column1: c41386|Know the Main Parts

e391bd|The core of VEX IQ: the Brain runs programs; Smart Motors move the wheels and arms; sensors (Distance, Color, Gyro, Bumper Switch, Touch LED) let the robot "know" its surroundings; the Controller is for driving by hand.
d5a18f|Ports and Wiring

d6b8a5|The Brain has 12 Smart Ports. Whichever port a motor or sensor is plugged into, set the same port number in VEXcode's Devices. When two motors are mounted facing opposite directions on the left and right sides, one of them must be set to Reverse.
324c3e|Download and Run a Program

b32b68|After writing a program you must Download it to the Brain before it can run on the robot without the computer. At a competition you pick the program to run on the Brain. If the battery is low, motors weaken and behave unpredictably, so charge it fully before competing.
05b4a5|VEXcode Basics

063ba5|VEXcode blocks are grouped by color (Drivetrain, Sound, Looks, Sensing, Inertial, Control, Operators, Variables…; categories for a device appear only after you add it). A program runs only if it starts from when started. To use a sensor, add it in Devices first. To try a different approach, use Save as to keep the old version, and note the difference in your notebook.
d5ced5|Beams, Pins and Sturdy Structures

bf44be|A triangle is the most stable structure; a four-sided frame easily skews. A diagonal brace turns a four-sided frame into two triangles. A joint with only one pin wobbles; fixing it at two or more points is steadier. Put heavy parts low and near the middle so the robot is less likely to tip over.
0d5032|Wheels and How Far You Go

e4be34|One turn of a wheel moves the robot about one circumference.
Distance = turns × circumference; turns = distance ÷ circumference.
Circumference = diameter × π (use π = 3.14).
175f97|Gear Ratio

4abf04|Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions. A small gear driving a big gear: slower, more force (reduction); a big gear driving a small gear: faster, less force (speed-up).
Driven turns = driving turns × driving teeth ÷ driven teeth.
0c77ed|Drivetrain and Turning

7f3afd|Two-wheel (or four-wheel) differential drive: when the left and right wheels spin the same direction at the same speed the robot goes straight; spinning them in opposite directions turns it in place. If the speeds differ, it veers toward the slower side. Omni wheels can slide sideways and have less resistance when turning in place. A 180° turn needs twice as much wheel rotation as a 90° turn.
2dcf68|Arms and Claws

0648b2|To lift something heavy: use reduction to trade speed for force. The longer the arm, the harder it is at the tip (a longer lever arm). A claw surface made of a high-friction material like rubber is less likely to let things slip. Follow the design process: find the need → think of ideas → build a prototype → test → improve.
639062|Programs Run in Order

535ca6|A program runs from top to bottom, one block at a time.
drive forward for 200 mm makes the robot go forward; turn right for 90 degrees turns it right 90 degrees. A different order makes the robot take a different path.
⚠ The Chinese VEXcode interface translates "right" as 「正確的」 (literally "correct"), so 「正確的」 = turn right and 「左邊」 = turn left.
04f97e|Turning Angles

289517|turn left / right turns the robot left / right, followed by the angle. 90° is a right angle, 180° is a U-turn, 360° is a full spin. To drive a square, turn 90° at every corner; to drive an equilateral triangle, turn 120° at every corner (not 60°, because what you turn is the "exterior angle").
d605de|Speed and Waiting

7c343a|set drive velocity to 50 % sets the speed. Speed affects only how fast, not the distance (the distance is decided by the number after "for"). wait 2 seconds pauses the program. If you go too fast, inertia makes the robot slide when it stops and causes errors.
7165fc|Repeat Blocks

1f5b03|repeat 4 repeats the blocks inside 4 times. To drive a square, put "drive + turn right 90" inside repeat 4 instead of writing 8 lines. Loops can be nested inside loops; the total counts multiply.
2db574|Forever, Events and Loop Conditions

3fdcca|forever repeats forever and never ends. To "keep doing something until something happens", use repeat until or while with a condition. Event blocks (for example "when Bumper pressed") can wait alongside the main program and react at any time.
00ec31|Conditions (if)
321ec8|if <condition> then: the blocks inside run only if the condition is true; else runs when it is false. and needs both sides true; or needs only one. Watch the direction of < and >.
48c86e|Distance Sensor

000288|The Distance Sensor measures the distance from the sensor to the object ahead. It's often used for "stop when near the wall". Robots have inertia and sensors have delay, so leave some room in the threshold, or slow down.
23a1f1|Bumper Switch and Touch

601118|The Bumper Switch detects whether it is pressed / bumped; the Touch LED detects touch and shows a light color. You can use wait until <Bumper pressed?> to "start only after a press", or to back up after hitting a wall.
3f9413|Color Sensor

e2333b|The Color Sensor recognizes colors and brightness. If it's too far away or the ambient light is too bright it becomes inaccurate, so test at a fixed distance under fixed lighting. To sort several colors use if … else if … else.
2f2525|Gyro Sensor

e656ea|The Gyro measures which way the robot faces / how many degrees it has turned. Run calibrate when the program starts, and keep the robot perfectly still. When wheels slip, turning with the Gyro is more accurate than counting wheel turns. The 2nd-generation Brain also has a built-in inertial sensor (VEXcode's "Inertial" blocks, e.g. BrainInertial heading), so you can measure heading even without a separate Gyro.
26f460|Variables
87252a|A variable is a named box that holds a number that can change. set score to 0 sets it to 0; change score by 1 adds 1 to the current number (it doesn't set it to 1).
97c68c|Operators and Comparisons
316306|+ − × ÷ can work out distance and time. Make units match first: 1 cm = 10 mm. Time = distance ÷ speed. and / or combine several conditions.
d6cda1|My Blocks (custom blocks)

4d4ed8|A My Block wraps a group of blocks you use often into one (press "Make a Block" in "Operators – My Blocks"), then you just call it. Benefits: reuse, and change one place and everything updates. A parameter (for example distance) lets the same block take a different number each time.
b4f6a4|Debugging and Competition Strategy

be9e31|Good debugging habits: observe → guess the cause → change only one thing → retest → record. Write test results in your engineering notebook; judges care about it. For strategy, get one scoring task working reliably first, then add more; don't write everything at once.
f132a4|Level Up Scoring

6b2e72|Bean bags score when thrown into goals: floor 1, L1 3, L2 6, L3 12, L4 16. A bean bag counts only if it's the same color as the goal or yellow; L4 takes only yellow. A bean bag counted at several levels scores only at the highest one. For the full rules see "Competition Zone → This Season: Level Up".
cd6711|Score Planning (runs and time)

35677e|You can handle only one bean bag at a time, so one run is one chance to score. 60 seconds ÷ seconds per run = the most runs; score = runs × points per bean bag. Higher levels score more but usually take longer per run — compare "total score", not a single run. You must measure these times; the times in the questions are only assumptions.
cc694b|Season Rules and Robot Limits

7d1e29|Teamwork: two robots, 1 minute, no autonomous period. Skills: 1 minute of driving + 1 minute of autonomous program (no controller during autonomous), ranked by the total of both runs. The robot must fit inside 11"×20"×15" and use at most 6 Smart Motors.
a1f37d|Driving Straight and Feedback (P Control)

8e8ce1|A robot told to "drive straight" often slowly drifts: the two motors and wheels never run at exactly the same speed. The fix is feedback: use the Gyro to measure the current heading, compute the error = target − current, then adjust the speed difference between the left and right wheels. The simplest way is P control: correction = Kp × error. Do this inside a repeat loop all the time, because the drift builds up as the robot moves. A Kp that is too small cannot correct enough; one that is too large makes the robot wobble (oscillate). PID goes further by adding I (handles a small error that never goes away) and D (brakes when the error changes too fast). Try it yourself in "Competition → Control Lab".
892ca3|Odometry and Accumulating Error

36c679|Odometry uses how far the wheels have turned to work out the robot's position and heading. Distance each wheel travelled: forward = (left + right) ÷ 2; turn angle = (right − left) ÷ track width (in radians). Equal distances = straight; the right wheel travelling farther = turning left. Drawback: wheel slip, uneven mats and wheel-size errors add up step by step, so the longer it runs, the less accurate it gets. That is why teams often combine it with a Gyro to correct the heading. See how error accumulates in "Competition → Control Lab".
